newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION - Bleak prospects for Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Bleak prospects for Hong Kong.

text.p: By Dr Markus Taube, China expert at the Ifo economic research institute in Munich.

MUNICH, March 26 - In less than one hundred days Great Britain will hand over its crown colony Hong Kong to the supremacy of the People's Republic of China. The prospects for Hong Kong's economic development under Chinese rule are mixed. In the short term it can be assumed that Hong Kong's gross domestic product will continue to achieve real growth rates of five to six percent. However, it is doubtful whether Hong Kong's growth dynamism can be maintained in the medium term.
Primarily, two facts speak for a positive assessment of Hong Kong's short-term development:

(1) Hong Kong's reintegration into the Chinese state organisation has to be seen in relation to Chinese policy on Taiwan. Hong Kong's return will serve as a model for the reunification with Taiwan desired by China. For this reason China will try to make it clear to the Taiwanese population that it has no reason to fear any negative effects on economic development if Taiwan were to reunite with China by preserving Hong Kong's material prosperity and economic efficiency.

The development on the Hong Kong stock exchange should also be judged against this background. The Hang Seng Index gained 34 percent in 1996 and has continued to rise to high levels in the first months of the current year. However, at the moment a stock market index's capacity to act as a forward-looking early warning system has been completely taken away from the Hang Seng Index. In its efforts to create the impression of a prospering Hong Kong economy even in the course of the change of sovereignty, the People's Republic of China has transferred capital to Hong Kong and thus ensured that the Hang Seng Index shows a positive development. China's interest in not allowing the Hang Seng Index to drop will probably determine the market in the coming months.

(2) The People's Republic of China has a very strong self- interest in Hong Kong. With an accumulated investment volume of more than 40 billion US dollars, China has become the most important country of origin for foreign direct investments in Hong Kong. The numerous Chinese capitalised companies in Hong Kong earn a substantial amount of foreign currency and provide a contact to the global market. In doing so, they fulfil an important function for the Chinese economy. Destabilisation in Hong Kong would severely interfere with this.

The ifo institute expects an increase in Hong Kong's real gross domestic product of 5.4 percent in 1997. This renewed rise in the growth rate will be supported by clear growth in private consumption, increasing capital investment and a revival of the export industry. The rate of inflation will rise provisionally by 0.7 percentage points to approximately 6.7 percent. The annual unemployment rate will probably remain stable, while the foreign currency reserves will grow again.

During the transition period, massive support from China will allow the former crown colony Hong Kong to maintain the status quo. However, as global interest begins to wane, China's Hong Kong policy will shift, which justifies doubts as to whether the positive development will continue in the medium term.

Beijing will start to exert its influence on the Hong Kong regional government more strongly and push for social and economic structures that suit the Chinese leadership. In the same way, the massive presence of Chinese companies will endanger the current "laissez faire" economic order. Chinese companies have not only actively endeavoured to expand their presence in strategically important sectors recently, they also mostly have close contacts to the political decision makers in the People's Republic of China. These are the perfect conditions to cultivate the germ cells of market dominating monopolies and to provide a gateway for nepotism and corruption, which can undermine the existing competitive order.

In addition to that Hong Kong has home-made structural problems to contend with. Up to now, the workforce made redundant in the course of the relocation of wage intensive production plants to the Chinese hinterland have been reaccomodated primarily in second-tier manufacturing positions or in service industry jobs, which are closely linked to the increased flow of goods caused by the production relocation.

The whole economy is therefore still based on those work intensive "low-tech" industries, which already dominated Hong Kong's economy two decades ago. The existing complementary structures between Hong Kong and Guangdong will be broken off to the same degree that the Chinese cooperation partners are able to develop their know-how in product design, marketing etc. through increasing direct contacts to the global market and to the degree they are able to fall back upon local finance and export services.

If, however, Hong Kong is no longer able to make a significant contribution towards the integration of Chinese companies in the global market, Hong Kong will become dispensable as a cooperation partner and as an economic location. Only if Hong Kong is able to preserve its specific, independent function in the Chinese economy, will it be able to continue to demand (economic and) political autonomy from the central government in Beijing as a result of its economic significance.

Hong Kong has indeed been able to consolidate its position as a regional financial centre, but this alone will not be enough to safeguard the city's prosperity in the future. In order to maintain economic dependence and to reduce its susceptibility to falls in demand, a strong, internationally competitive industrial sector is indispensible as the second supporting pillar of the economy beside a universally employable service sector. The building up of own "high-tech" industries is urgently needed. Singapore has already shown that this is also possible in a city state. In Hong Kong, however, there has been hardly any sign up to now that structural change modelled on the Singapore example will be introduced.
